sense: an earnest call for help or support

terms.gloss: appeal to, call on for help; plead for
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; the person, or the help asked for (auxilium, fidem), in the accusative
evidence: Cic. Flacc. 4 (Lewis & Short): quem enim alium appellem? quem obtester? quem implōrem?
Cic. Quinct. 94 (Lewis & Short): cujus hominis fidēs implōranda est?
terms.comment: Festus explains it as asking with tears (Lewis & Short): an urgent appeal, to gods or to people. Fidem alicujus implōrāre, to appeal to someone’s good faith; auxilium implōrāre, to appeal for help.

evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.5.188 (Lewis & Short): vōs etiam atque etiam implōrō et appellō
terms.comment: To go up to someone and speak to them, so also to call on them for help; its commoner senses are to address and to name (see address). In law, to appeal to a magistrate (see appeal, to a higher court).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent; often with ut or nē + subjunctive
terms.comment: To beg by all that is sacred, calling gods or men to witness; it stands beside implōrō in Cic. Flacc. 4 and Verr. 2.5.188 (Lewis & Short). For a plain “please”, see please.

phrases.latin: quem enim alium appellem? quem obtester? quem implōrem?
phrases.english: For to whom else should I appeal? Whom should I beseech? On whom should I call for help?

phrases.latin: mulierēs … quae ad proelium proficiscentēs mīlitēs passīs manibus flentēs implōrābant nē sē in servitūtem Rōmānīs trāderent
phrases.english: the women, … who with outstretched hands and in tears implored the soldiers setting out for battle not to hand them over to the Romans as slaves

sources: Lewis & Short: imploro · Lewis & Short: appello · Lewis & Short: obtestor
